Chapter 7: Challenging the Fear of Making Mistakes.
Have you ever held back from trying something new, just because you were worried about making a mistake?
You’re definitely not alone. For so many of us, that fear can run deep. It often shows up as perfectionism, procrastination, or even just hesitating to step out of our comfort zone.
When you get right down to it, this fear is usually tied to how we see ourselves—like, if we mess up, it somehow means we’re not good enough, or that we’ve failed in some way.
But here’s something to think about: What if mistakes weren’t the enemy?
Imagine looking at every misstep as a natural, even necessary, part of growing. Remember how kids learn to walk? They don’t just stand up and get it perfect—they stumble, fall, and keep getting back up. That’s how real learning happens, even for adults. Mistakes aren’t proof that we’re weak; they’re actually stepping stones, helping us get better and understand more along the way.
So, how do you start challenging that fear of making mistakes? Well, try these ideas:
First, see each error as feedback—not a judgment on who you are.
Next, practice a little self-compassion. Talk to yourself the way you’d encourage a friend who’s just starting something new.
And finally, set expectations that are actually realistic. Nobody’s perfect, and honestly, perfection isn’t even the goal.
Here’s a metaphor I love: Picture a sculptor working on a statue. Every chip, every adjustment, gets the piece closer to what it’s meant to be. It’s messy, it’s imperfect, but it’s all part of the process of creating something amazing.
In real life, this could mean volunteering for a new project at work, even if you’re not sure you’ll nail it. Or maybe trying a creative hobby, just for the fun of it—without stressing about the end result. Each time you give yourself permission to try—and maybe even stumble—you’re building resilience and confidence for whatever comes next.
So, here’s the key takeaway: When you start seeing mistakes as chances to learn, not as threats, you break free from that perfectionist trap.
You open yourself up to a life that’s richer, more adventurous, and honestly, a whole lot more fun.
